\title{What Belongs in an Agent's Context Window?}

\author{Neil Lunavat}
\affiliation{%
  \institution{Pimpri Chinchwad College of Engineering}
  \country{India}}
\email{neillunavat3192@gmail.com}

\begin{abstract}
An LLM-based coding agent operates within a finite context window, and before it edits a file in an unfamiliar repository, it must therefore determine which other content to include in that window. Given the file being changed, this article compares the two signals that existing tools rely on for this selection --- proximity in the import graph and the text of the issue report --- as well as their fusion. The comparison covers 2{,}412 change tasks drawn from 1{,}162 pull requests in 112 Python repositories, and each reading order is evaluated by how much of an answer key it covers per line read.

The main contribution of this article is a measurement protocol. Benchmarks constructed from issue reports conflate two regimes, because in two tasks in five the issue names a file that the change touches. Stratifying tasks by such naming, comparing each ordering against an issue-free twin, and deleting only the names from the same issue together allow these two regimes to be separated. Applying this protocol, we find that the issue contributes $+0.156$ AUC to the best ordering when it names a key file, compared with a non-significant $+0.016$ otherwise, and that approximately half of this difference is attributable to the naming itself. A dense code retriever makes better use of the issue, but the same two-regime pattern remains. Under the same controls, the apparent competition between graph-based and text-based signals disappears, and a human-annotated key agrees with the patch-derived key that the field already adopts. Our practical recommendation is to fuse a walk from the file with issue retrieval: this ordering held under predictions committed before scoring on seven unseen repositories and on the human-annotated key, as well as when the file to be changed must itself be identified. All experiments in this study run without paid model access; we specify, but do not conduct, the end-to-end agent experiment.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{LLM agents, context windows, code search, context retrieval, dependency graphs, benchmark validity, empirical
software engineering}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

Consider an LLM coding agent that is given a bug report and a file to change. Before it can produce any edit, it must decide which additional content to place in its context window, and including everything is not an option. In the corpus we study, the median pull request targets a repository of 286{,}385 tokens (counting the Python files in the import graph and excluding tests and non-Python files), and 74.8\% of pull requests target a repository larger than a 128{,}000-token window. The files that contain the answer account for a median of 2.98\% of the repository. A selection step is therefore unavoidable.

Two signals are available for this selection. The dominant one in tool development is the dependency graph: Aider constructs a repository map from definitions and references, and RepoGraph, LocAgent and CoSIL traverse a code graph outward from a starting point, based on the premise that the information needed is located near the code being changed. The other signal is the issue report, which SWE-bench's own retrieval baseline queries with BM25~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and which every agent reads. In this article, we compare the two signals, and their fusion, as \emph{reading orders} evaluated by how much of an answer key they cover per line read. In every task, the reader is given the file being changed, and the question is which \emph{other} files to read. Our focus is therefore on retrieval rather than repair.

A naive version of this comparison is straightforward to conduct but yields misleading conclusions. When evaluated against the files co-edited in the pull request, issue text performs best; when evaluated against the files that define symbols used by the change, structure performs best, and the ranking of methods is nearly inverted. However, neither half of this result survives two controls. The structural half reflects a population effect: a symbol key exists for single-file changes, whereas a co-edited key does not, so the two keys are scored on different pull requests. The lexical half is largely explained by the issue naming the answer: in two tasks in five, the issue names a changed file as code, which a method that matches issue words against file paths can read off directly. Furthermore, a human-annotated key agrees with the co-edited key.

Two findings survive these controls, and this article is organised around them. The first concerns the benchmark more than the methods. Issue-aware retrieval is substantially more valuable on issues that name their files, and a within-task redaction experiment quantifies how much of this value is due to the names themselves. We use the term \emph{leakage} for these names only in this benchmark sense: in deployment, an issue that names \texttt{core.py} is a legitimate input, but an average over issues that do and do not name their files describes neither case, and the proportion between them varies across corpora. The second finding is a recommendation: fusing a walk from the file with issue retrieval is robust across keys, strata, unseen repositories, a human-annotated key, alternative cost rules and the loss of the free seed, with the exception of single-file changes, for which the walk alone performs better.

\paragraph{Research questions.}
\begin{description}
\item[RQ1] Does the uncontrolled comparison between structural and lexical reading orders still hold after the populations are matched and issues that name the answer are controlled for?
\item[RQ2] How much value does issue text contribute to retrieval, and how much of this value stems from the issue naming the files to be changed?
\item[RQ3] Which ordering is robust, and does its performance hold on unseen repositories, on a human-annotated key, under other cost rules, and without a free seed?
\item[RQ4] Beyond this, what does the import graph contribute?
\end{description}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A protocol for measuring the value of issue text.} An issue-free twin of each ordering captures the total value of the issue, and three nested within-task redactions isolate the portion carried by content that points at the key files. On issues that name a key file as code, the issue contributes $+0.156$ AUC to the best fusion, of which 0.061 to 0.078 is attributable to the names; on the remaining issues, it contributes $+0.016$. A dense retriever makes better use of the issue, but the same pattern holds (Section~\ref{sec:issue}).
\item \textbf{A robust recommendation, validated out of sample.} Reciprocal-rank fusion of a personalised walk with issue retrieval is never significantly worse than the best pure ordering on the matched population. It held under predictions committed before scoring on seven unseen repositories and on ContextBench's human-annotated key, and it remains the best ordering without a free seed. Whether the walk should favour short files depends on how a context is charged (Section~\ref{sec:robust}).
\item \textbf{Controls that altered conclusions in this study}: matching the populations on which two keys are scored; stratifying by whether the issue names a key file as code; and treating the repository as the unit of analysis, which preserves the significance of the headline comparisons but changes the significance verdict for 102 of the 1{,}076 comparisons that are significant with the pull request as the unit (none of which changes sign).
\item \textbf{Corrections to common arguments in favour of graph retrieval.} The two-hop neighbourhood contains, on average, 87.5\% of the needed files and 56\% of the repository. Walking against import edges is costly, whereas discarding edge direction is not. Moreover, the advantage that structure shows on a key built from imports is not corroborated by a human-annotated key (Section~\ref{sec:graph}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Structure and history as guides to change.} Impact analysis~\cite{bohner1996impact} propagates a change from a modified element along its dependencies; Robillard~\cite{robillard2008topology} ranks program elements according to dependency topology; and surveys of feature location~\cite{dit2013featurelocation} observe that structural, textual and dynamic techniques are typically evaluated in isolation. Furthermore, Ko et al.~\cite{ko2006exploratory} observed that developers navigate largely by names and search. Co-change mining~\cite{ying2004predicting,zimmermann2004mining} suggests files that tend to change together; our co-edited key adopts this notion as ground truth rather than as a method.

\paragraph{Graph-based context for agents.} SWE-bench~\cite{jimenez2024swebench} and its successors~\cite{badertdinov2025swerebench,zhang2025swebenchlive} established repository-scale change tasks as a standard benchmark, and a family of systems assembles context by traversing a code graph: Aider's repository map~\cite{aider2023repomap}, RepoGraph~\cite{ouyang2025repograph}, LocAgent~\cite{chen2025locagent} and CoSIL~\cite{jiang2025cosil}. In contrast, Agentless~\cite{xia2025agentless} relies on file and directory names. Table~\ref{tab:priorkeys} lists the ground truth against which each system is evaluated, as reported in its own evaluation section. Almost all of them use the files touched by the gold patch (i.e., our co-edited key), and our results support this choice: of our two proxies, it is the one with which a human-annotated key agrees. However, none of them reports results separately for issues that do and do not name the files being scored.

\paragraph{Issues that reveal the answer.} SWE-Bench+~\cite{aleithan2024swebenchplus} finds that 32.67\% of the passing patches produced by SWE-Agent with GPT-4 had the solution in the issue or its comments, and Agentless reports issues that contain the exact patch. A weaker form of this leakage concerns only \emph{location}: a retrieval step needs only to know which files to open. This form is also known. Agentless classifies the location information in SWE-bench Lite and finds that around half of its issues already provide the location of the file to be edited. Similarly, the SWE-Bench Illusion study~\cite{liang2025illusion} shows that models identify the buggy file from the issue alone in up to 76\% of SWE-bench Verified tasks, compared with 53\% on repositories outside SWE-bench. Our rate, 40.2\% of tasks naming a key file as code, is consistent with the first of these findings. Our contribution is not the rate itself but its consequence: how much of an issue-aware method's score it accounts for, separated within each task from the rest of the issue's content.

\paragraph{Concurrent work on the key.} SWE-Explore~\cite{zhang2026sweexplore} derives ground truth from the code that successful agents read and scores ranked lists under a line budget, which is close to our cost model; ContextBench~\cite{li2026contextbench} annotates gold context manually; AgentRetrievalBench~\cite{qin2026agentretrievalbench} scores files according to whether they help the next step; and GraphLocator~\cite{liu2025graphlocator} dual-annotates the patch-derived key. We use ContextBench's key as a third, independent answer key (Section~\ref{sec:robust}).

\section{Study Design}
\label{sec:design-freeze}

The corpus, graph builder, task definition and metric were fixed and tagged in version control before any method was run (the \emph{design freeze}). The method families, including the fusion among them, were added afterwards in response to the first results; the fusion therefore originated as an exploratory result. We subsequently tested it twice under predictions committed to the repository before any of the data they concern were scored (\texttt{paper/external\_predictions.md}, \texttt{paper/contextbench\_predictions.md}). Because a signed tag in our own repository establishes order only for a reader who trusts the repository, we do not describe either step as a pre-registration. Analyses that were added in response to review and were not fixed in advance (the cost rules, the dense retriever, the systems' selectors and the condition without a free seed) are marked as exploratory where they appear. Every change made after results existed is logged in the replication package.

\subsection{Corpus, tasks and keys}

\begin{sloppypar}
We drew 1{,}886 pull requests from SWE-bench, SWE-bench-Live and SWE-rebench in Python repositories that satisfy our sampling rules, with at most 20 per repository. A pull request that edits $k$ existing non-test source files that are nodes of the import graph yields $k$ tasks: each edited file in turn serves as the \emph{seed}, and the task is to order the remaining files of the repository. This procedure yields 3{,}123 tasks from 1{,}873 pull requests in 113 repositories (13 pull requests edit no graph file). Of these, 2{,}412 tasks (1{,}162 pull requests in 112 repositories) have at least one key file once the seed is removed, and only these tasks are scored. Of the 711 unscored tasks, 706 originate from pull requests that change a single source file; they account for 61.2\% of all 1{,}154 such tasks, because the symbol key described below is empty whenever the changed code resolves to nothing outside itself. In the median task, the repository has 131 graph nodes and the key contains 2 files.
\end{sloppypar}

Graphs are constructed for each base commit using an \texttt{ast} walker: nodes are source files, an edge $a \rightarrow b$ indicates that $a$ imports a module resolving to $b$, test files are excluded, and the per-file line counts obtained in the same pass serve as the cost unit. We define two keys, which are never merged:

\begin{description}
\item[\m{co\_edited}] The other non-test source files changed by the same pull request, representing what a developer actually touched, independently of the import graph. This key is available only when a pull request edits more than one graph file: 1{,}958 tasks from 708 pull requests.
\item[\m{symbol}] Files that define names used on the lines added by the pull request, resolved with \texttt{jedi}'s \texttt{goto} using \texttt{follow\_imports=True} on the patched code, representing what the change depends on. This key covers 2{,}341 tasks from 1{,}156 pull requests.
\end{description}

\noindent Because the symbol key is constructed by following imports, it is partly circular with respect to the structural orderings, and we therefore treat it as the secondary proxy. The 702 pull requests that carry both keys constitute the \emph{matched population}, on which every cross-key comparison is repeated. Of the 1{,}156 pull requests with a symbol key, 454 have no co-edited key because they edit a single graph file; we refer to these as \emph{single-file} pull requests. By \emph{issue text}, we refer to the problem statement only, excluding the maintainers' \texttt{hints\_text}.

A third key, used only in Section~\ref{sec:robust}, is ContextBench's human-annotated gold context~\cite{li2026contextbench}: the Python files that an annotator judged necessary to reconstruct the fix, excluding the seed. We processed its SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro Python tasks through the unchanged pipeline, sampled according to our sampling rules: 108 pull requests in 14 repositories have a non-empty gold key, 6 of which are also in the main sample.

\subsection{Reading orders}

Every ordering receives the graph, the seed, per-file identifier bags and the issue text, and ranks every other file (Table~\ref{tab:methods}). Identifier bags are obtained by splitting identifiers on underscores and camel case, and the issue is tokenised in the same way. BM25 uses $k_1 = 1.5$, $b = 0.75$ and differs across methods only in the query. Fusion is performed with reciprocal-rank fusion (RRF) with $k = 60$. Variants with the suffix \texttt{\_pl} divide a score by file length. Four orderings recur throughout this article, and in the text we refer to them by plain names: \emph{the fusion} (\texttt{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path}), \emph{the length-aware walk} (\texttt{ppr\_und\_pl}), \emph{the hop walk} (\texttt{hops\_lines}) and \emph{path matching} (\texttt{path\_issue}). Note that structural orderings are given a correct seed, whereas issue orderings receive no seed at all.

Three further kinds of ordering were added after review; they are scored but excluded from the ranks and correction families of the other tables, so that their addition does not change any result reported elsewhere. First, a \emph{dense retriever}, \texttt{jina-embeddings-v2-base-code} (the model our design fixed before any method was run), ranks files by the cosine similarity between their first 512 tokens and the issue (\texttt{dense\_issue}), which is embedded as a whole as the length-weighted mean of its 512-token chunks. Its fusions replace or complement BM25 over contents. Second, the \emph{issue-free twins} of the fusions replace every issue-derived input with its seed-derived counterpart. Third, the \emph{context selectors of three published systems} (Aider's repository map, RepoGraph's two-hop ego graph and LocAgent's typed breadth-first search, reimplemented from their papers) are scored as orderings, with the files they do not select appended in random order.

\subsection{Metric}

An ordering is read from the top, one whole file at a time, until the next file would exceed the line budget. Coverage is defined as the fraction of the key that has been read. We evaluate at budgets ranging from 250 to 32{,}000 lines in doublings and report the AUC, i.e., the mean coverage over the eight budgets; ties are re-drawn three times and the results are averaged. Python source averages 8.50 tokens per line in aggregate over the 121{,}075 distinct file versions (\texttt{cl100k\_base}), so a budget of 8{,}000 lines corresponds to roughly 68{,}000 tokens. Restricting the AUC to budgets of up to 8{,}000 lines does not change the leading orderings.

Because AUC has no intuitive scale, we anchor it as follows. On the matched population, a random ordering scores 0.249 and the oracle 0.774 on the co-edited key (0.252 and 0.779 on the symbol key), so a difference of 0.05 AUC corresponds to about a tenth of the distance from random to oracle; the recommended fusion covers 45\% of this distance on the co-edited key and 41\% on the symbol key. We also report the number of lines read before half of the key is covered (Table~\ref{tab:lines} in the appendix).

The rule that reading stops at the first file that overflows the budget is part of the frozen metric. Because this rule favours short files, Section~\ref{sec:robust} additionally scores every ordering under a rule that skips such a file and continues reading, and under a rule that charges each file one unit regardless of its length.

\subsection{Statistics}
\label{sec:stats}

Task AUCs are first averaged within each pull request. Paired comparisons use the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with the repository as the unit of analysis (i.e., pull-request scores averaged within each of the 112 repositories), because pull requests are clustered in repositories that differ in size, layout and issue-writing culture. Effect sizes are reported as Vargha--Delaney $A_{12}$, and confidence intervals are obtained by bootstrapping over repositories. Holm correction is applied within families fixed by the design (Table~\ref{tab:families}): each combination of key, unit, population and leakage stratum constitutes one family of 325 tests among twenty-six orderings. Ranks are computed among the twenty-two ranked orderings, excluding the oracle, so that the best ordering is ranked first. Differences quoted in the text are taken from the repository-level Wilcoxon analysis; they are means of per-repository differences and can therefore differ in the third decimal from the pull-request means reported in the tables. The mixed-model estimates of the same comparisons are reported in Table~\ref{tab:mixed} and can differ slightly from them.

The choice of unit matters for borderline comparisons: of the 1{,}076 comparisons that are significant after Holm correction with the pull request as the unit, 102 are not significant with the repository as the unit, and the reverse holds for 2. No estimate changes sign. In addition, every comparison on which a claim rests is re-estimated as a linear mixed model of the per-pull-request difference with a random intercept per repository (Table~\ref{tab:mixed}); for 40 of these 41 comparisons, the mixed model reaches the same verdict. The exception is the comparison between the hop walk and path matching on co-edited files, for which the mixed model finds path matching better by 0.044 ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$), whereas the repository-level test does not; no claim depends on this comparison being null.

\section{Results}

\subsection{RQ1: the naive comparison and why it does not hold under controls}
\label{sec:naive}

Table~\ref{tab:main} presents the comparison as it is commonly conducted: each key over its full population, without any control. Under the co-edited key, the five best orderings comprise four fusions and one lexical method, and the best purely structural ordering ranks ninth. Under the symbol key, the four best orderings comprise three structural orderings and one fusion, and the best lexical ordering ranks fourteenth. The individual reversals are large and significant: path matching outperforms the length-aware walk by 0.059 AUC on co-edited files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$) but underperforms it by 0.100 on symbol files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-7}$). Taken at face value, these results indicate that the choice of key determines which signal performs best.

\paragraph{The structural half of this reversal reflects a population effect.} The two columns are scored on different pull requests: 454 of the pull requests in the symbol column are single-file changes, which have no co-edited key and are precisely the cases in which a seed's import neighbourhood contains most of what there is to find. On the 702 pull requests that carry both keys (Table~\ref{tab:shared}), we observe that nothing changes on the co-edited key, whereas on the symbol key a walk along import edges falls from first to seventh (0.491 to 0.417) and path matching rises from fourteenth to eighth. The same comparison that gave the walk a 0.101 lead on the full corpus ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-7}$) yields $+0.008$ and $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$ on the matched population; for the hop walk against path matching, it yields $+0.019$ and $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$. Consequently, the top three places under both keys are held by the same three fusions.

\paragraph{The lexical half is largely explained by the issue naming the answer.} The full path of a key file appears verbatim in the issue for 12.6\% of tasks, and its bare stem for 48.5\%. A stem written as code (\texttt{core.py}, \texttt{simbad/core}, a dotted module path, inside backticks or within a code block) is referred to as an \emph{explicit} mention, and a stem written only as an ordinary word as an \emph{incidental} mention. Explicit mentions occur in 40.2\% of tasks. Removing them, together with applying the population control (Table~\ref{tab:leak}), moves path matching on co-edited files from fifth to twelfth and pure structure from ninth to fifth. In addition, the advantage of the hop walk over path matching changes from $-0.007$ under the full-path control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$) to $+0.042$ under the primary control ($p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.60$), on 531 pull requests. As a result, the ordering that appeared to be the best single signal on this key becomes indistinguishable from one that never reads the issue. The issue does not name the seed file more often than the key files, so the seed does not explain this effect: its full path appears in 10.3\% of tasks.

\paragraph{Which proxy to trust.} In cases where the two keys still disagree, a human-annotated key provides the deciding evidence. On ContextBench's tasks, it agrees with the co-edited key: the ranking under the human key agrees with that of the co-edited key at Kendall $\tau = 0.97$ and with that of the symbol key at 0.59. Moreover, the length-aware walks that rank first and fourth under the symbol key rank tenth and fourteenth under the human key (Table~\ref{tab:cbauc}). Therefore, the answer to RQ1 is negative: once the populations are matched and the naming is controlled, neither signal family dominates, and the key that the field already uses is the better of the two proxies. The remainder of this section examines how much the issue is then worth and which ordering is safe to use.

\subsection{RQ2: the value of the issue and the contribution of the names}
\label{sec:issue}

Stratifying by whether the issue names a key file compares two kinds of issue in addition to two degrees of leakage: a report that contains a stack trace is plausibly longer and more tractable than a one-line feature request. We therefore measure the value of the issue twice, once across tasks and once within tasks.

\paragraph{Across tasks: an issue-free twin.} Each fusion is paired with a twin in which every issue-derived input is replaced by its seed-derived counterpart; for example, \texttt{rrf\_pprpl\_issue\_path} is paired with \texttt{rrf\_pprpl\_seedpath}, which fuses the same walk with the same two BM25 rankings queried by the seed's own path and contents. The twin combines the same number of lists but never reads the issue, so the difference between the two measures the value of the issue, net of the effect that ``a fusion simply receives more input''. On the matched population, the issue contributes $+0.069$ AUC to the fusion on the co-edited key and $+0.055$ on the symbol key. On tasks whose issue names a key file as code, these values increase to $+0.156$ and $+0.121$; on the remaining tasks, they are $+0.016$ and $+0.012$, and neither survives correction.

\paragraph{Within task: redaction.} We then take the \emph{same} issue and delete the content that points at the key files, while preserving the prose, the traceback and the length. Because what counts as ``pointing'' is a design choice, we define it in three ways. Specifically, the \emph{names} arm deletes only explicit mentions of the key files' stems; the \emph{paths} arm additionally deletes every component of their paths; and the \emph{symbols} arm additionally deletes every function, class and method name that they define, in each case only where written as code. The names arm provides a lower bound on leakage, whereas the wider arms over-remove content, since a directory called \texttt{models} is also ordinary vocabulary; the three arms therefore bracket the effect. Of the 970 tasks whose issues name a key file, the 848 in the matched population (378 pull requests in 105 repositories) are scored. Removing only the names reduces the AUC of path matching by 0.110 on co-edited files and that of the fusion by 0.061; the wider arms reduce the fusion's AUC by 0.084 and 0.096 (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}). On the issues that name nothing, the names arm has no effect, as expected by construction, whereas the wider arms reduce AUC by 0.016 to 0.018, which corresponds to the part they over-remove.

\paragraph{The decomposition.} Because both experiments run on the same population with the same unit, their results are additive. On issues that name a key file, the issue contributes $+0.156$ to the fusion on co-edited files; on the remaining issues, it contributes $+0.016$. Of this $+0.140$ gap, the names arm attributes 0.061 to the names, and the widest arm, net of what it also removes where nothing is named, attributes 0.078 (on the symbol key, 0.050 to 0.065 of a $+0.109$ gap). Hence, between two fifths and a half of the difference between the two kinds of issue is due to the naming itself. The remainder reflects a difference between the issues, or between the tasks, that none of the redactions we could define captures: even path matching, which reads only file paths, scores 0.393 on named-file tasks after the widest redaction, compared with 0.333 on the other tasks.

\paragraph{A better reader.} All of the above analyses read the issue with BM25, so ``what the issue is worth'' could characterise the retriever rather than the issue. The dense retriever makes better use of the issue: on its own, it exceeds BM25 over contents by 0.059 and 0.054, and when substituted for BM25 in the fusion, it adds 0.018 on both keys (Table~\ref{tab:dense}). On issues that name nothing, the dense fusion gains 0.033 from the issue on co-edited files, twice the gain of the BM25 fusion and, unlike it, statistically significant; on the symbol key, it gains 0.017, which is not significant. Part of the small value of unnamed issues was therefore attributable to BM25. However, this gain is still a fifth of what the same fusion gains where the issue names a file (0.178), and the names account for a similar share: of the 0.145 stratum gap, 40 to 47 per cent, compared with 43 to 56 per cent for BM25. We did not evaluate a reader that processes the issue as a whole, such as an LLM reranker; the redaction protocol applies to such a reader without modification.

\paragraph{What these results imply.} They do not imply that issue text is useless: an ordering that exploits a real report naming a real file exploits information that genuinely exists. Rather, they show that a benchmark assembled from issue reports measures two regimes simultaneously, in proportions that vary across corpora, and that these regimes can be separated at the cost of a few regular expressions and one additional run. Consequently, any evaluation on SWE-bench-derived data that reports a gain from issue-aware retrieval without the stratification and the redaction reports the sum of the two.

\subsection{RQ3: a robust ordering and its generalisability}
\label{sec:robust}

If the answer key is not known in advance (and for a tool shipped to users, it is not), the quantity to optimise is the worst-case performance of a method across keys, measured as its shortfall behind the best ordering under either key. On the matched population, the best ordering by this criterion is the fusion, which is the best ordering under both keys; it exceeds the best pure lexical ordering by 0.055 and 0.067 and the best pure structural ordering by 0.097 and 0.039. It is never significantly worse than the best pure ordering in any leakage stratum on the matched population. On the full symbol-key population, however, it is: once issues that name a key file are removed, the length-aware walks outperform it by 0.049 to 0.062 ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$), because that population retains the single-file pull requests. On these pull requests, the five best orderings are all structural, and for a change that touches one file, the walk alone is the better choice.

Because the fusion was identified after the results had been observed, we tested it further. Table~\ref{tab:robust} reports every test, and Table~\ref{tab:pred} lists the eight predictions committed before scoring.

\paragraph{Held-out repositories.} Across 200 random 56/56 splits of the repositories, a mechanical selection criterion applied to one half selects the fusion in 198 splits. In 195 of these, it is the best ordering on the co-edited key of the other half, and in 198 of 198 on the symbol key (Table~\ref{tab:heldout}). This result demonstrates that the choice is stable across our repositories, but it does not demonstrate that the choice generalises.

\paragraph{Seven unseen repositories.} Seven repositories satisfy all of our sampling rules and were excluded only because their tasks originate from SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Pro. We drew 140 pull requests from them according to the same rules and committed four predictions before building anything. Three of these predictions hold: the fusion ranks second under both keys, behind only another fusion built on the hop walk, with a worst-case shortfall of 0.030 (exactly at the limit we set rather than within it); it is never significantly worse than a pure ordering; and walking inward is as costly as in the main sample. The fourth prediction fails: deleting the names reduces the fusion's AUC by 0.030 on the co-edited key with $p_{\text{Holm}} = 0.11$, on only 33 matched pull requests in six repositories, so the causal effect of the names alone is not established for this set. The wider arms reduce it by 0.086 and 0.090: in these larger repositories, issues refer to files through their directories more than through their names.

\paragraph{A human-annotated key.} On ContextBench's tasks, all four predictions hold. The fusion is the second-best ordering on the human key, 0.009 behind a fusion of the same family, and it achieves a higher AUC than each of four named pure orderings, by 0.086 to 0.128 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.008$). Its annotators worked from the fix, and 108 pull requests constitute a small set; nevertheless, it is the only key in this article that was not constructed by any part of our pipeline.

\paragraph{Other cost rules.} Under the frozen rule, preferring short files approximates a knapsack heuristic for the metric, so the length-aware walk could owe its position to the rule itself. Under a rule that skips a file that does not fit and continues reading, the fusion is the best ordering on the symbol key and 0.002 behind the fusion built on the hop walk on the co-edited key. However, the margin gained from length-awareness shrinks by about sixty per cent (the two fusions that differ only in this respect differ by $+0.015$ and $+0.021$ instead of $+0.042$ and $+0.050$). Under a rule that charges each file one unit, length-awareness becomes a disadvantage, and the unscaled fusion \texttt{rrf\_ppr\_issue\_path} is the best ordering under both keys. In summary, a fusion is the best ordering under every rule; whether its walk should favour short files depends on whether a context is charged by size, as a token window is, or by the number of files opened (Table~\ref{tab:metric}).

\paragraph{Without a free seed.} In practice, an agent is not given the file to change. For each pull request, we therefore let the issue select the seed (the top-ranked file of the dense retriever), walk from that guess and fuse, and we score the result against every edited file (including the true seeds, so that identifying the file is part of the task) and against the symbol key. The guess is the correct file in only 34\% of pull requests; nevertheless, walking from it and fusing with the dense reader yields the best ordering under both keys, at 0.516 and 0.475 (Table~\ref{tab:seedless}). It outperforms the dense retriever alone by 0.023 on the edited files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-3}$) and 0.058 on the symbol key, and ties with it where the issue names no edited file ($-0.001$). Seeding the walk with a BM25 guess instead, which is correct in 41\% of pull requests, performs worse, which indicates that the reader that selects the seed should be the same reader that reads the issue in the fusion.

\paragraph{Published systems' selectors.} When scored as orderings on the matched population, the context selectors of Aider, RepoGraph and LocAgent rank between tenth and twentieth. The recommended fusion exceeds each of them by 0.115 to 0.176 on co-edited files and by 0.084 to 0.155 on symbol files ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-4}$). Aider's repository map and RepoGraph's two-hop ego graph also rank below the plain length-aware walk, while LocAgent's typed search ties with it on co-edited files. Note that these are the selectors alone, reimplemented from the original papers without the language model that each system wraps around them; the comparison therefore reflects what their graph component contributes as a reading order, not how well the systems perform.

\paragraph{The fusion's own parameter.} The RRF parameter $k$ was fixed at 60 without prior testing; at $k = 10$ and $k = 200$, the fusion's AUC changes by at most 0.007 on the co-edited key and 0.010 on the symbol key.

\subsection{RQ4: the contribution of the import graph}
\label{sec:graph}

\paragraph{The two-hop neighbourhood covers half of the repository.} Specifically, 86.7\% of symbol-key files and 88.1\% of co-edited files lie within two undirected hops of the seed (Table~\ref{tab:distance}), which at first sight appears to be strong evidence in favour of graph retrieval. However, the median two-hop ball contains 68 files and about 21{,}600 lines, more than five times a 4{,}000-line budget. Relative to its own repository, it covers a median of 58.5\% (a mean of 56\%), with a median precision of 3.4\%, and it improves recall over a random sample of the same size by a factor of only 1.57. The two-hop neighbourhood is therefore not an effective filter: it indicates only that the needed files lie somewhere within half of the repository, which is precisely where the \emph{ordering} determines the outcome.

\paragraph{Direction: reversing a walk is costly, whereas discarding direction is free.} Walking along import edges, towards what the seed depends on, places \texttt{ppr\_out\_pl} first on the symbol key at 0.491, whereas walking against them drops to 0.277 (twentieth), a gap of 0.215 on the full population ($p_{\text{Holm}} < 10^{-14}$). The undirected walk loses almost nothing (0.489). On the co-edited key, every directed walk ranks below \texttt{same\_dir}, which consults no graph at all. Because the symbol key is constructed by resolving names along imports in one direction, a walk in that direction measures something close to the key's own construction.

\paragraph{The contribution of a repository prior.} A query-independent PageRank, which never considers the seed or the issue, reaches 0.410 on symbol files compared with 0.491 for the best personalised walk (67\% of the walk's margin over random), but only 0.271 on co-edited files, barely above random (0.248), where the walk exceeds it by 0.101. This indicates that knowing which file is being changed matters considerably for predicting what else was changed, and much less for predicting what the code calls.

\paragraph{The signals retrieve different files.} At $k = 20$, 24.4\% of co-edited files are found only by the lexical family and 9.5\% only by the structural family; on symbol files, the asymmetry is reversed (20.0\% against 16.5\%, Table~\ref{tab:comp}). This complementarity explains why fusing the two families is effective; where the issue names a key file, much of the lexical family's share is attributable to that naming (Section~\ref{sec:issue}).

\paragraph{What the human key reveals about the graph.} On the gold files that a fix reads but does not edit (the context that a graph walk is supposed to be best at finding), walks and issue-only retrievers are indistinguishable on the 85 ContextBench pull requests that contain such files (differences of 0.006 to 0.012, $p_{\text{Holm}} = 1$), and the fusion outperforms the issue-only orderings by 0.082 and 0.084 ($p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.008$). Note that this analysis was added after the predictions were scored.

\paragraph{The budget is rarely the binding constraint.} An oracle fits the complete key within 8{,}000 lines for 97.5\% of pull requests, whereas the best ordering completes 58.5\% on the co-edited key and 51.0\% on the symbol key (Table~\ref{tab:full}). Because the oracle reads only key files, the forty-point gap is an upper bound on what a better ordering could add rather than an estimate; what it establishes is that an ordering that fails to cover the key at this budget fails because of its order.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for benchmarks.} The field's default key, namely the files touched by the gold patch, is the better of our two proxies: a human-annotated key agrees with it rather than with the key built from imports. The field's omission lies elsewhere. In this corpus, two tasks in five have an issue that names a key file as code, and the score of an issue-aware method mixes that regime with the other. The control requires only a regular expression over text that the benchmark already provides, and the redaction requires one additional run. We believe that retrieval results on issue-derived benchmarks should report the naming rate, the stratified result and the redaction as routinely as the corpus size.

\paragraph{Implications for tools.} Tool builders should fuse a walk from the file being changed with issue retrieval, read the issue as effectively as possible (in our study, a dense retriever outperforms BM25), and make the walk favour short files only if the context is charged by size. For a change confined to one file, the walk alone is the better choice. When the file to change is not known, the same reader should select the starting point. The two-hop neighbourhood is not a useful filter on its own, and direction matters only insofar as walking against imports is costly.

\paragraph{What the baselines do not show.} Our orderings are deliberately simple (BM25, PageRank and one embedding model), and the systems' selectors are reimplemented from their papers rather than run end to end. A skeptical reader could interpret the fusion result as two weak but complementary signals outperforming each signal alone. We acknowledge that this interpretation is accurate; the value of the fusion lies in its robustness, its low cost and the fact that it survives every test we could devise. The methodological contribution does not depend on it: the stratification and redaction protocol applies to any reader of the issue, including an LLM reranker, which we did not evaluate.

\paragraph{Scope and remaining work.} Every experiment in this article runs on a CPU without paid model access, and within this budget we extended the evaluation as far as possible: two proxy keys, a human key, unseen repositories, a dense retriever, three systems' selectors, and a condition without the free seed. What these experiments cannot show is whether better retrieval increases the rate at which an agent resolves the issue. Answering this question requires model calls at scale, and Appendix~\ref{sec:protocol} specifies the experiment in advance so that it can be run without modification. Its analysis would inherit the protocol introduced in this article (stratifying by naming, the issue-free twin, the redaction and the repository as the unit), which constitutes the contribution we offer here.

\paragraph{Recommendations.} (1) Report retrieval results separately for each answer key, and prefer the patch key over an import-derived key. (2) Report, and stratify by, whether the query names the answer files as code, and apply the redaction to any method that reads the issue. (3) Compare each issue-aware method against the same method with a seed-derived query. (4) Match the populations before comparing results across keys. (5) Cluster statistical tests by repository. (6) State explicitly how reading is charged.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{Construct validity.} Neither proxy key constitutes ground truth about what a developer needed to read. The co-edited key conflates files changed with files read; the symbol key is circular with respect to the structural orderings; and the human key covers 108 pull requests and records what the fix required as reconstructed by annotators who had seen the fix. Coverage assumes that whole files are read; the alternative cost rules indicate which conclusions depend on this assumption.

\paragraph{Internal validity.} The graph builder does not capture dynamic imports or plugin registration. The symbol key inherits \texttt{jedi}'s resolution failures, which depend on the environment: rebuilding the keys of all 1{,}886 sampled pull requests on a second machine left every co-edited key identical but changed the symbol key of 41 pull requests, typically by one file. Re-scoring changes no AUC by more than 0.003 and alters no conclusion. In the held-out splits of Section~\ref{sec:robust}, the fusion is then selected in 194 of 200 splits instead of 198, and confirmed on the co-edited key in 191 of these instead of 195. This article reports the keys as originally built. The leakage classifier is a regular expression and will mislabel some mentions, which is why we report three nested strata and three redaction arms. Leakage that we did not anticipate redacting, such as a paraphrase of a function's behaviour, would remain in the residual; the leakage share is therefore bounded more firmly from below than from above.

\paragraph{External validity.} Our study is limited to Python and to file granularity, and its pull requests come from benchmarks that select for reproducible, test-verified fixes, which may be better documented than average and may therefore overstate the effectiveness of issue-text methods. Very large repositories are under-represented; nevertheless, the pattern in Table~\ref{tab:main} is stable across size quartiles (Table~\ref{tab:size}). Finally, the external set comprises seven repositories, and one of its four predictions failed.

\paragraph{Conclusion validity.} The fusion family was selected after the results had been observed. The held-out splits, the external repositories and the human key test it, but none of them can undo the fact that we selected it, from five candidates, on these data.

\section{Conclusion}

What belongs in an agent's context window, given the file it is changing? When compared naively, import-graph proximity and issue-text matching exchange positions depending on the answer key. This reversal is a property of the comparison rather than of the signals: one half of it stems from the different pull requests that the two keys cover, and the other from the issues that name their files. Moreover, a human-annotated key agrees with the key that the field already uses. Two contributions survive: a protocol and a recommendation. Issue-aware retrieval is worth $+0.156$ AUC where the issue names a changed file, compared with a non-significant $+0.016$ elsewhere, and about half of this difference is due to the naming itself; benchmarks should therefore report the two regimes separately. Furthermore, fusing a walk from the file with issue retrieval is robust across keys, unseen repositories, a human key, cost rules and the loss of the free seed, with the exception of single-file changes, for which the walk alone performs better.

\section*{Data Availability}

The replication package contains the graphs, tasks, keys, issue bags, orderings and scores; the external and ContextBench trees together with the predictions committed before they were scored; the scripts that compute the dense embeddings, which are regenerated rather than distributed; and every analysis script. A checker recomputes every number quoted in the text from the result files and fails if any sentence disagrees with them. The package will be archived under a permanent identifier upon acceptance.

\section{A Protocol for the Downstream Test}
\label{sec:protocol}

Whether a context assembled by one of these orderings enables a model to fix the issue can only be determined by running models, which we have not done; we therefore specify the experiment here so that it can be run or refuted. \emph{Corpus}: the 1{,}162 scored pull requests, each with a benchmark test specification. \emph{Conditions}, each truncated to the same token budget of 16{,}000 or 64{,}000 tokens: (i) the seed alone; (ii) the seed plus \texttt{ppr\_und\_pl}; (iii) the seed plus \texttt{path\_issue}; (iv) the seed plus the recommended fusion; (v) the seed plus \texttt{rrf\_hops\_path}; (vi) the seed plus the issue-free twin of (iv); (vii) the repository in a fixed canonical order; (viii) the seed plus the key files, as an upper reference. \emph{Models}: two models of clearly different capability, with one API call per task and condition and no tools. \emph{Outcome}: a task is considered resolved if the patch applies and the specified tests pass; conditions are compared using a mixed-effects logistic regression with a random intercept per repository, with McNemar tests alongside and Holm correction across condition pairs. \emph{Pilot}: 150 tasks on the weaker model; if (viii) resolves fewer than 10\% or more than 90\% of tasks, the budget is adjusted and the adjustment is reported. If (ii)--(vi) do not differ from (vii), retrieval quality does not transfer to repair at these budgets; if (iv) does not outperform (vi), the issue does not justify its inclusion downstream either.
